title: Inequities in geographic access to emergency obstetric and newborn care in Greater Accra
methods: congestion-aware network travel time (Google Maps Directions API, GNN ETA model)
S2 level-14 discrete global grid tessellation
facility functionality survey (UNFPA Rapid EmONC Assessment Tool 2018)
data_sources: Ghana Health Service routine health data and facility register (CHIM)
UNFPA/AMDD Rapid EmONC Assessment Tool 2018 field survey

data_scope.facility_screening_criterion: >=3 cesarean births per month in 2023 (Ghana Health Service routine data)
data_scope.analysis_grid: S2 level-14 cells, approximately 600 m x 600 m (cell count not reported in article)
data_scope.wealth_travel_time_correlation: Pearson r = -0.48 (95% CI -0.49 to -0.47); authors note CI understates uncertainty due to spatial autocorrelation
data_scope.transport_mode_modeled: motorized driving only (GAR routine-care mode split is approximately 54% motorized / 46% non-motorized)
not_reported: facility queueing/capacity in the accessibility model

core_conclusion: Under peak traffic the median travel time to the nearest public comprehensive EmONC facility in Greater Accra is 29.7 minutes, sitting on the 30-minute clinical danger threshold. Aggregate coverage looks adequate (about 90% of women aged 15-49 within 30 minutes of public care, 93% including private) but conceals a steep wealth gradient (poorest quintile 40.3 min vs wealthiest 15.4 min, Pearson r = -0.48) and a congestion-induced access cliff: 5.7% of women have at least one reachable public facility off-peak and none at peak, with peri-urban districts such as Ga South, Shai Osudoku and Ningo/Prampram carrying almost all the deficit.
why_it_matters: Shows that geographic access to life-saving obstetric care is time-varying rather than a static map property, so conventional cost-friction accessibility products overstate coverage in congested African cities; converts the deficit into an actionable headcount (92,952 less-wealthy women more than 30 minutes from public comprehensive EmONC at peak); demonstrates that private-sector supply concentrates where wealth already is and does not close peri-urban gaps; and challenges the assumption of an urban health advantage in rapidly urbanizing sub-Saharan Africa.
why_nature: Couples urban form and traffic dynamics directly to a life-or-death health outcome, the core Nature Cities thesis; advances measurement by replacing friction-surface modelling with congestion-aware ML-based routing that corrects a known threefold overestimation of coverage in LMIC settings; quantifies equity rather than asserting it via satellite-derived relative wealth; addresses Global South urban science where most future urban growth will occur; and releases a reusable geospatial accessibility database plus replication code as research infrastructure.
